title: Inequality and the Limits of Growth
text:
Economic inequality is often measured by the gap between the highest and lowest incomes within a society. Although many countries have grown wealthier over recent decades, the benefits of that growth have not been distributed evenly. In several nations, a small share of the population now controls a disproportionate part of total wealth. Such concentration, economists argue, can undermine social mobility and weaken public trust.

Defenders of market-based policies, however, contend that inequality is a natural consequence of rewarding talent and effort. They point out that progressive taxation and generous welfare programmes may discourage investment and innovation. Critics respond that unchecked disparities create lasting barriers for children born into poorer households. The debate, therefore, is less about whether inequality exists than about how much of it a society can tolerate.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, how is economic inequality often measured?
options: By the gap between the highest and lowest incomes
By the number of people living abroad
By the average age of workers
By the level of public school spending

questions.text: What do defenders of market-based policies say about progressive taxation?
options: It may discourage investment and innovation
It has no effect on investment
It is required by international law

questions.text: What can be inferred about the author's view of the debate?
options: The author sees the question as one of degree rather than existence.
The author believes inequality does not exist in modern societies.
The author supports removing all taxes.
The author considers the debate settled in favour of the critics.

questions.text: Why might a high concentration of wealth weaken social mobility?
options: Children from poorer households face lasting barriers to advancement.
Wealthy families are required to share their savings.
Public trust increases when fewer people own property.

paragraph_translations: La desigualdad económica suele medirse por la diferencia entre los ingresos más altos y los más bajos dentro de una sociedad. Aunque muchos países se han enriquecido en las últimas décadas, los beneficios de ese crecimiento no se han repartido de manera equitativa. En varias naciones, una pequeña parte de la población controla ahora una parte desproporcionada de la riqueza total. Según los economistas, esa concentración puede socavar la movilidad social y debilitar la confianza pública.

Los defensores de las políticas basadas en el mercado, sin embargo, sostienen que la desigualdad es una consecuencia natural de recompensar el talento y el esfuerzo. Señalan que los impuestos progresivos y los programas de bienestar generosos pueden desalentar la inversión y la innovación. Los críticos responden que las disparidades sin control crean barreras duraderas para los niños nacidos en hogares más pobres. Por tanto, el debate no trata tanto de si existe la desigualdad, sino de cuánta de ella puede tolerar una sociedad.
